title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
keyIdea: Keep ans, where ans[k] = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1 (always sorted). A number bigger than ans.back() extends it; otherwise binary-search the first ans[k] ≥ it and replace. The size of ans is the answer: O(n log n).

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: At each index: take it (if it's bigger than the previous taken one) or skip it.
approaches.why: Two choices per index with no saving; the stack goes n deep.

approaches.name: Memoization
approaches.idea: Same take/skip recursion; state (curr, prev) saved in dp[curr][prev + 1] (prev = -1 means nothing taken yet, hence the + 1).
approaches.why: n × (n + 1) states, O(1) each; the table is n + 1 by n + 1.

approaches.name: Tabulation
approaches.idea: Fill dp[curr][prev + 1] from curr = n − 1 down and prev = curr − 1 down to −1, reading the row below; answer dp[0][0].
approaches.why: Two nested loops over curr and prev; the full table is (n + 1)².

approaches.name: Tabulation, two rows
approaches.idea: Each row only reads the row below, so keep currrow and nextrow.
approaches.why: Same loops; only two rows of n + 1.

approaches.name: Binary search with lower_bound
approaches.idea: Your commented version: the tails array, with lower_bound finding the first ans[k] ≥ num[i].
approaches.why: n numbers, one O(log n) lower_bound each; ans has at most n entries.

approaches.name: Binary search (tails array)
approaches.idea: Your active code: push when num[i] > ans.back(), else your binarySearch returns the first ans[k] ≥ num[i] and you replace it.
approaches.why: n numbers, one O(log n) binary search each over the sorted tails; ans has at most n entries.

quiz.q: What does ans[k] mean in the binary search method?
options: The smallest number that can end an increasing subsequence of length k + 1
The k-th number of the LIS
How many numbers are smaller than nums[k]
The LIS ending at index k

quiz.q: Is ans at the end always a real increasing subsequence of nums?
options: No, only its length is guaranteed

quiz.q: Why search for the first value ≥ x (not > x)?
options: The subsequence must be strictly increasing, so an equal value replaces rather than extends

quiz.q: In the memo version, why dp[curr][prev + 1]?
options: prev can be −1 (nothing taken yet), so shift it by 1 to get a valid index
To leave room for the answer
